lesson.title: Two equations, two unknowns
points: A pair of linear equations in x and y has the form a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0. Its solution is a pair (x, y) that satisfies both equations together.

On a graph the pair is two straight lines. If they cross, there is exactly one solution. If they are parallel, there is no solution. If they lie on top of each other, there are infinitely many solutions.
Compare the ratios: a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2 gives one solution. a1/a2 = b1/b2 ≠ c1/c2 gives none. a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2 gives infinitely many.
To solve, use substitution or elimination: make the coefficient of one variable the same in both equations, then add or subtract to remove it.
lesson.story: At a mela, one stall sells 2 samosas and 1 chai for ₹25, and another sells 1 samosa and 1 chai for ₹15. Each stall gives one equation, and only one price for each item fits both bills.

lesson.title: Equations with x squared
points: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 where a ≠ 0. It can have at most two roots.
To solve by factorisation, split the middle term bx into two terms whose product is ac and whose sum is b. Then use: if p × q = 0, then p = 0 or q = 0.
The quadratic formula is x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The expression D = b² − 4ac is called the discriminant.
If D > 0 there are two distinct real roots. If D = 0 the two roots are equal. If D < 0 there are no real roots.
lesson.story: A farmer has a rectangular plot whose length is 3 m more than its breadth and whose area is 70 m². Writing area = length × breadth gives x(x + 3) = 70, which is a quadratic equation in the breadth x.

lesson.title: Steps of equal size
points: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers where each term is got by adding the same number d to the term before it. d is called the common difference.
In the list a, a + d, a + 2d, ... the nth term is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]. It can also be written Sₙ = n/2 (first term + last term).
To test for an AP, subtract each term from the next. If the answer is always the same, it is an AP.

lesson.title: Same shape, different size
points: Two triangles are similar if their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are in the same ratio. They have the same shape but not always the same size.
Tests for similarity: AA (two angles equal), SSS (three pairs of sides in the same ratio) and SAS (one angle equal and the sides around it in the same ratio).

Basic Proportionality Theorem: a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio. The ratio of the areas of two similar triangles is the square of the ratio of their corresponding sides.
In a right-angled triangle, (hypotenuse)² = (side 1)² + (side 2)². This is the Pythagoras theorem.

lesson.title: Ratios in a right triangle
points: In a right-angled triangle, for an acute angle θ, the side opposite θ is the opposite side, the side next to θ is the adjacent side, and the longest side is the hypotenuse.
sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent. Because of similar triangles, these ratios depend only on the angle and not on the size of the triangle.
For every angle, sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight to something above.
lesson.story: A kite flies on a taut string 50 m long, and the string makes an angle of 30° with the ground. The kite's height is the side opposite the angle, so height = 50 × sin 30° = 50 × 1/2 = 25 m, without climbing anything to measure it.

lesson.title: Solids joined together
points: A combined solid is made by joining solids such as a cone, cylinder and hemisphere. Its volume is the sum of the volumes of the parts.
For the surface area, add only the surfaces you can see from outside. The faces where two solids are joined are hidden, so they are not counted.
Cylinder: V = πr²h, curved area 2πrh. Cone: V = 1/3 πr²h, curved area πrl, where l = √(r² + h²). Sphere: V = 4/3 πr³, area 4πr². Hemisphere: V = 2/3 πr³, curved area 2πr².
When a solid is melted and recast into another shape, its volume stays the same. Its surface area does change.
lesson.story: A capsule in a medicine strip is a cylinder with a half-ball (hemisphere) at each end. Its shiny coating covers the curved surfaces only. The circles where the hemispheres meet the cylinder are inside, so they get no coating and are not counted.

lesson.title: Chance and averages
points: Probability of an event E = (number of outcomes favourable to E) ÷ (total number of equally likely outcomes). It always lies from 0 (impossible) to 1 (sure), and P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

lesson.title: Reactions and balanced equations
points: In a chemical reaction old substances change into new substances. Signs include a change in colour, a gas given off, a precipitate forming, or a change in temperature.
A chemical equation must be balanced: the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides, because mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction.

Main types are combination (A + B → AB), decomposition (AB → A + B), displacement (a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one) and double displacement (two compounds exchange ions). Reactions that give out heat are exothermic and those that absorb heat are endothermic.
Gain of oxygen (or loss of hydrogen) is oxidation, and loss of oxygen (or gain of hydrogen) is reduction. Rusting of iron and rancidity of oils are everyday oxidation changes.

lesson.title: Metals, non-metals and reactivity
points: Metals are usually shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals are usually brittle and poor conductors. Exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal, graphite conducts electricity, and diamond is the hardest natural substance.
The reactivity series, from most to least reactive, is K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

Oxides of Al and Zn are amphoteric because they react with both acids and bases. Alloys such as brass, bronze and steel are mixtures of metals with improved properties.

o.m: Assumed carbon can reduce any metal oxide, but carbon is less reactive than these metals

o.t: Heating their oxides alone in air
o.m: Assumed that heating alone is enough, which works only for metals low in the series like mercury

o.t: Displacement by copper from their salt solutions
o.m: Assumed a less reactive metal can displace them, but only a more reactive metal can

lesson.title: Carbon: bonds, series and reactions
points: Carbon has 4 electrons in its outer shell. It is tetravalent and forms four covalent bonds by sharing electrons. It can join to other carbon atoms in long chains (catenation). Diamond, graphite and fullerene are allotropes of carbon.
Hydrocarbons: alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (single bonds), alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (a double bond) and alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (a triple bond). Members of a homologous series differ by a CH₂ unit, which is 14 u.

Functional groups: alcohol –OH, aldehyde –CHO, ketone >C=O and carboxylic acid –COOH. Ethanol reacts with sodium to give hydrogen. Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate to give carbon dioxide and with ethanol to give a sweet-smelling ester.
Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids. They clean by forming micelles around oil. In hard water they form an insoluble scum with calcium and magnesium salts.
lesson.story: In a kitchen, LPG burns with a clean blue flame, while a ghee lamp or candle gives a yellow, sooty flame. Both are carbon compounds, but the saturated gas burns cleanly and the unsaturated, carbon-rich fuels give soot.

example.q: Write the molecular formulae of the alkane and the alkene that have 4 carbon atoms.
steps: Alkane: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 4 gives C₄H₁₀ (2 × 4 + 2 = 10).
Alkene: CₙH₂ₙ with n = 4 gives C₄H₈ (2 × 4 = 8).
So butane is C₄H₁₀ and butene is C₄H₈.

qs.q: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom normally form?
qs.why: Carbon has 4 electrons in its outer shell and shares all four, so it forms four covalent bonds.

o.m: Counted the electrons in the first shell of carbon instead of its outer shell
Confused carbon with nitrogen, which has a valency of 3
Used the octet of 8 electrons as the number of bonds instead of the number of electrons shared

qs.q: What is the general formula of alkanes?
qs.why: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, for example CH₄ and C₂H₆.

o.m: Used the general formula of alkenes
Used the general formula of alkynes
Guessed that carbon and hydrogen atoms are equal in number

qs.q: A hydrocarbon has the molecular formula C₃H₄. To which family does it belong?
qs.why: For 3 carbons, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ gives 2 × 3 − 2 = 4 hydrogen atoms. So C₃H₄ is an alkyne.

o.m: Took any hydrocarbon to be an alkane without checking hydrogen against 2n + 2 = 8
Used 2n = 6 hydrogen atoms for an alkene and did not notice only 4 are present
Ignored that an alcohol needs an –OH group, while C₃H₄ has only carbon and hydrogen

qs.q: Which functional group is present in ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH)?
qs.why: Ethanoic acid contains the carboxylic acid group –COOH.

o.m: Noticed only the OH at the end and ignored the C=O next to it
Confused the –COOH group with the aldehyde group because both have a C=O
Saw the C=O and ignored the –OH attached to the same carbon

qs.q: Which pair of compounds belongs to the same homologous series?
qs.why: Propane (C₃H₈) and butane (C₄H₁₀) are both alkanes and differ by one CH₂ unit.

o.m: Thought equal carbon numbers put compounds in one series, but ethane and ethene have different bonding
Thought the same number of carbon atoms means the same series, but the functional groups differ
Thought a one-carbon difference of any kind is enough, but the functional groups differ

qs.q: The molecular mass of butane (C₄H₁₀) is 58 u. What is the molecular mass of pentane (C₅H₁₂)? (C = 12, H = 1)
qs.why: Pentane has one more CH₂ unit: 58 + 14 = 72 u. Check: 5 × 12 + 12 × 1 = 72.

o.m: Added only the mass of a carbon atom (12) and forgot the two extra hydrogen atoms
Added 16 for a CH₄ unit instead of 14 for a CH₂ unit
Added 28, the mass of two CH₂ units, for one more carbon atom

qs.q: Sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to a colourless liquid. There is brisk fizzing, and the gas turns lime water milky. Which liquid is it most likely to be?
qs.why: Only acids release carbon dioxide from hydrogencarbonates. Of the options, ethanoic acid is the acid.

o.m: Thought the –OH of an alcohol makes it react with hydrogencarbonate like an acid
Thought any carbon compound with an –OH group gives CO₂ with hydrogencarbonate
Thought water reacts with hydrogencarbonate to give CO₂, but a neutral liquid does not

qs.q: Why does soap form a scum instead of a good lather in hard water?
qs.why: Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts. These react with soap to form an insoluble scum.

o.t: Sodium chloride in the water destroys the soap
o.m: Thought common salt in water spoils soap, but the problem is calcium and magnesium salts

o.t: Soap cannot dissolve in any kind of water
o.m: Thought soap works only in distilled water, but soft water gives plenty of lather

o.t: Hard water is acidic and turns the soap into acid
o.m: Confused hardness with acidity, but it is caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium salts

o.t: Calcium and magnesium salts react with soap to form insoluble scum

lesson.title: Life processes in plants and humans
points: Nutrition: green plants make food by photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, using sunlight and chlorophyll. Gases enter through stomata. In humans, saliva, gastric juice (HCl and pepsin), bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice digest food, and villi absorb it.
Respiration: glucose is broken down to release energy as ATP. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and gives CO₂ and water. Anaerobic respiration gives ethanol and CO₂ in yeast and lactic acid in muscles.

Transport: the human heart has four chambers and blood passes through it twice in one round (double circulation). Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it back. In plants, xylem carries water and minerals upwards and phloem carries food to all parts.
Excretion: each kidney has many nephrons. Blood is filtered in the glomerulus, useful substances are reabsorbed, and the wastes leave as urine through the ureter, bladder and urethra.
lesson.story: If you chew a plain piece of roti for a minute, it begins to taste slightly sweet. Your saliva contains an enzyme that starts breaking starch into sugar before the food even reaches the stomach.

example.q: Trace the path of oxygen-rich blood in the human heart after it leaves the lungs.
steps: Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through the pulmonary veins.
It passes to the left ventricle, which has a thick muscular wall.
The left ventricle pumps it into the aorta, which carries it to the whole body.

qs.q: In which part of the cell does most of the energy release of aerobic respiration take place?
qs.why: Mitochondria are called the powerhouses of the cell because most ATP is produced there.

o.m: Confused respiration, which releases energy, with photosynthesis, which captures it in chloroplasts
Thought the control centre of the cell also produces its energy
Mixed up making proteins with releasing energy from glucose

qs.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
qs.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins bring blood back to the heart.

o.m: Mixed up the direction of flow and thought veins carry blood away from the heart
Picked the thinnest vessels, which join arteries to veins and exchange materials
Confused blood circulation with the lymph system, which collects tissue fluid

qs.q: Why does a roti taste sweeter the longer you chew it?
qs.why: Saliva contains salivary amylase, which breaks starch in the roti into sugar (maltose).

o.t: Salivary amylase breaks starch into sugar
Chewing alone turns starch into sugar
o.m: Thought crushing food physically changes starch into sugar, but an enzyme is needed

o.t: Saliva has hydrochloric acid that makes sugar
o.m: Mixed up saliva with gastric juice, which has HCl, and thought acid forms sugar

o.t: Roti already contains a lot of sugar that is slowly released
o.m: Thought the sweetness is stored sugar and ignored that wheat flour is mostly starch

qs.q: Which part of the nephron in the kidney filters the blood?
qs.why: The glomerulus is a cluster of thin-walled capillaries in the cup-shaped Bowman's capsule, where blood is filtered.

o.m: Thought the tube that carries urine from kidney to bladder does the filtering
Thought the organ that stores urine also filters blood
Thought the tube that passes urine out of the body does the filtering

qs.q: After a fast sprint, the leg muscles ache because of the build-up of which substance?
qs.why: When oxygen is short, muscle cells break down pyruvate to form lactic acid. Its build-up causes cramps and pain.

o.m: Thought anaerobic respiration always gives ethanol, which is true only for yeast
Gave the products of aerobic respiration even though oxygen was short
Mixed up the waste of protein breakdown, excreted by the kidneys, with muscle respiration

qs.q: During photosynthesis in a leaf, 3 molecules of glucose are formed. How many molecules of CO₂ were used? (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂)
qs.why: Each glucose needs 6 CO₂. So 3 glucose molecules need 3 × 6 = 18 CO₂ molecules.

o.m: Matched each glucose molecule with one CO₂ molecule, ignoring the coefficient 6
Used the CO₂ needed for one glucose and forgot to multiply by 3
Added 6 and 3 instead of multiplying

qs.q: Which is the correct path of blood that has just returned from the lungs?
qs.why: Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium, moves to the left ventricle and is pumped into the aorta.

o.t: Lungs → right atrium → right ventricle → aorta
o.m: Mixed up the sides; the right side of the heart handles blood coming from the body

o.t: Body → left atrium → left ventricle → lungs
o.m: Reversed the circuit, as blood from the body goes to the right side and then to the lungs

o.t: Lungs → left ventricle → left atrium → aorta
o.m: Reversed the order of chambers; blood enters the atrium first and then the ventricle

o.t: Lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta

qs.q: Which statement about transport in plants is correct?
qs.why: Xylem carries water and minerals from roots to leaves. Phloem carries the food made in leaves to other parts.

o.t: Xylem carries food from leaves, and phloem carries water from roots
o.m: Swapped the jobs of xylem and phloem

o.t: Xylem carries water and minerals upward, and phloem carries food from leaves to other parts
Both xylem and phloem carry only water
o.m: Thought plants need to transport only water and ignored the food made in leaves

o.t: Phloem carries water upward by transpiration pull
o.m: Mixed up the transpiration pull in xylem with food transport in phloem

lesson.title: Mirrors, lenses and refraction
points: Light follows the laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A concave mirror converges light and a convex mirror diverges it. The focal length is half the radius of curvature, f = R/2.

Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, and magnification m = −v/u. With the sign convention, distances are measured from the pole, and a real object in front of the mirror has u negative. A concave mirror has f negative and a convex mirror has f positive.
Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another. Refractive index n = c/v, where c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Light bends towards the normal when it enters a denser medium.
Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, with m = v/u. Power of a lens P = 1/f with f in metres, measured in dioptres (D). A convex lens has positive power and a concave lens has negative power.
lesson.story: The small mirror on a scooter shows a wide view of the road behind you with cars looking smaller. It is a convex mirror, which always forms a smaller, upright image and covers a large area.

example.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
steps: Sign convention: u = −30 cm and f = −10 cm.
The image is 15 cm in front of the mirror, real, inverted and half the size of the object.

qs.q: Which type of mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
qs.why: A convex mirror always gives an upright, smaller image and has a wide field of view, so the driver sees more of the road.

o.m: Thought a mirror that enlarges is better for seeing behind, but a concave mirror gives a narrow view
Thought a flat mirror is best because the image is the same size, but its field of view is small

o.t: Concave mirror, because it forms a real image
o.m: Thought a real image helps the driver, but a mirror that gives a wide view is needed

qs.q: What is the SI unit of the power of a lens?
qs.why: Power P = 1/f with f in metres, and its unit is the dioptre (D).

o.m: Confused power with focal length, which is measured in metres
Confused the power of a lens with electrical power
Confused the power of a lens with force

qs.q: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 24 cm. What is its focal length in magnitude?

o.m: Took the focal length to be equal to the radius of curvature
Doubled the radius instead of halving it
Halved the radius twice

qs.q: The speed of light in glass is 2 × 10⁸ m/s and in vacuum it is 3 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the refractive index of glass?

o.m: Divided the speed in glass by the speed in vacuum instead of the other way round
Added the two speed values instead of dividing them
Multiplied the two speed values instead of dividing them

qs.q: A ray of light goes from air into glass at an angle. How does it bend?
qs.why: Glass is optically denser than air. Light slows down in glass and bends towards the normal.

o.m: Mixed up the rule and thought light bends away when it slows down

o.t: It does not bend and goes straight
o.m: Thought light changes direction only at a mirror and not on entering glass

o.t: Along the surface of the glass
o.m: Confused refraction with the special case of total internal reflection at the critical angle

qs.q: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image and what is its nature?
qs.why: u = −30, f = −20. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 + 1/30 = −1/60, so v = −60 cm. m = −v/u = −2. The image is 60 cm in front of the mirror, real, inverted and magnified.

o.t: 12 cm in front of the mirror, real, inverted and diminished
o.m: Ignored the signs and added the reciprocals 1/20 + 1/30 to get 1/12

o.t: 60 cm behind the mirror, virtual, erect and magnified
o.m: Read the negative sign of v as meaning behind the mirror

o.t: 50 cm in front of the mirror, real, inverted and magnified
o.m: Added u and f instead of using the mirror formula

o.t: 60 cm in front of the mirror, real, inverted and magnified

qs.q: A diverging lens has a focal length of −50 cm. What is its power?

o.m: Ignored the negative sign, but a diverging lens has negative power
Used the focal length in centimetres instead of metres
Wrote the focal length in metres as the power without taking the reciprocal

qs.q: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image formed?
qs.why: u = −15, f = +10. 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, so v = +30 cm. The image is real and inverted on the other side of the lens (m = −2).

o.t: 6 cm on the same side as the object, virtual and erect
o.m: Added 1/10 and 1/15 using wrong signs to get 1/6, then misread the sign

o.t: 25 cm on the other side of the lens, real and inverted
o.m: Added u and f in size instead of using the lens formula

o.t: 30 cm on the same side as the object, virtual and erect
o.m: Got the distance right but misjudged the side, since a positive v means the far side of the lens

o.t: 30 cm on the other side of the lens, real and inverted

lesson.title: Current, resistance and power
points: Electric current I = Q/t, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 coulomb per second). Potential difference V = W/Q is measured in volts. An ammeter is connected in series and a voltmeter in parallel.
Ohm's law: V = IR. Resistance of a wire R = ρl/A, so it increases with length and decreases with area. Resistivity ρ depends on the material and temperature, not on the size of the wire.

Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + ..., the same current flows through each resistor. Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ..., the same potential difference is across each resistor, and the total resistance is less than the smallest one.
Heating effect H = I²Rt. Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R, measured in watts. One kilowatt hour (1 unit) = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. A fuse has a low melting point and melts when the current is too high.
lesson.story: During Diwali, a string of cheap series lights goes dark if one bulb fuses, as the current has no other path. The lights and fans in your house are in parallel, so each works even if another is switched off.

example.q: Resistors of 12 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel to a 12 V battery. Find the total current.
steps: For parallel resistors, R = (12 × 6)/(12 + 6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω.
Use Ohm's law: I = V/R.
Check: 12 V/12 Ω = 1 A and 12 V/6 Ω = 2 A, and 1 + 2 = 3 A.

qs.q: Which instrument measures electric current and how is it connected in a circuit?
qs.why: An ammeter measures current and is connected in series so that the whole current flows through it.

o.m: Knew the instrument but connected it across the component, which would short the circuit
Mixed up the voltmeter with the ammeter
Mixed up the voltmeter, which measures potential difference, with the ammeter

qs.q: Why is the wire used in an electric fuse made of a material with a low melting point?
qs.why: If the current becomes too large, the heating effect melts the fuse wire and breaks the circuit, protecting the appliances.

o.t: So that it can carry a very large current safely
o.m: Thought a fuse should withstand any current, but its job is to break the circuit

o.t: So that it has very high resistance and saves energy
o.m: Thought a fuse wire must have high resistance, but its role is protection

o.t: So that it melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too high
So that it becomes a magnet during a short circuit
o.m: Mixed up the heating effect with the magnetic effect of current

qs.q: A steady current of 2 A flows through a wire for 30 seconds. How much charge flows through it?

o.m: Divided the time by the current instead of multiplying
Added the current and the time
Subtracted the current from the time

qs.q: A heater draws a current of 5 A when connected to a 220 V supply. What is its resistance?

o.m: Multiplied V and I instead of dividing V by I
Added the voltage and the current
Divided I by V instead of V by I

qs.q: A wire of resistance R is replaced by another wire of the same material and same thickness but double the length. What is the new resistance?
qs.why: R = ρl/A. With the same ρ and A, doubling the length doubles the resistance to 2R.

o.m: Thought a longer wire conducts better and so has less resistance
Squared the change in length, but resistance is directly proportional to length
Thought resistance depends only on the material and not on the length

qs.q: Resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
qs.why: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω. This is less than the smaller resistor.

o.m: Added the resistances as if they were in series
Found 1/R = 1/2 correctly but forgot to invert it to get R
Took the average of the two resistances

qs.q: A 2 kW geyser is used for 30 minutes every day for 30 days. If one unit of electricity costs ₹6, what is the cost of running the geyser?
qs.why: Energy per day = 2 kW × 0.5 h = 1 kWh. For 30 days it is 30 units. Cost = 30 × 6 = ₹180.

o.m: Took the time as 1 hour per day instead of 30 minutes
Calculated the cost of just one day instead of 30 days
Used 30 minutes without converting it to hours

qs.q: A 6 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor and a 2 Ω resistor in series. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?
qs.why: Total R = 6 Ω, so I = 6/6 = 1 A. The potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor is V = IR = 1 × 4 = 4 V.

o.m: Split the battery voltage equally between the two resistors
Gave the full battery voltage to one resistor, but in series it is shared
Divided the battery voltage by 4 Ω instead of using the current

lesson.title: Heredity, Mendel and evolution
points: Offspring resemble their parents because traits are passed on through genes. Gregor Mendel studied pea plants. In a cross between pure tall (TT) and pure dwarf (tt) plants, all F1 plants are tall, and the F2 generation has tall and dwarf plants in the ratio 3 : 1.

A trait that shows in F1 is dominant and the one that is hidden is recessive. In a dihybrid cross (round yellow × wrinkled green seeds), F2 shows the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, so traits are inherited independently.

Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Females are XX and males are XY. All eggs carry X, and a sperm carries X or Y, so the father's sperm decides the sex of the child.

Variations that help survival are selected by nature, which is the basis of evolution. Homologous organs have the same basic structure but different functions (human arm and bat wing), while analogous organs have different structures but similar functions (wings of a bird and an insect). Fossils give evidence of evolution.
lesson.story: A child may have the mother's eyes and the father's curly hair, and cousins in a family can differ in height. Each trait is controlled by a pair of genes, one from each parent, and different combinations give variety.

example.q: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt) are crossed. Of 400 offspring, how many are expected to be dwarf?
steps: Gametes of each parent are T and t.
The offspring are TT, Tt, Tt and tt, in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1, which gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
Only tt plants are dwarf, which is 1 out of 4.
Expected dwarf plants = 1/4 × 400 = 100.

qs.q: Who is known as the father of genetics for his experiments on pea plants?
qs.why: Gregor Johann Mendel did experiments on pea plants and gave the basic laws of inheritance.

o.m: Mixed up the scientist of natural selection and evolution with the one who studied inheritance
Mixed up the discoverer of cells with the scientist of inheritance
Mixed up the scientist known for germ theory with the scientist of inheritance

qs.q: How many pairs of chromosomes are there in a normal human body cell?
qs.why: A human cell has 46 chromosomes, which is 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.

o.m: Took the total number of chromosomes as the number of pairs
Counted only the autosomes and left out the sex chromosomes
Added one extra pair for each sex chromosome

qs.q: What decides whether a human baby will be a boy or a girl?
qs.why: All eggs carry an X chromosome. A sperm carries either X (girl, XX) or Y (boy, XY), so the sperm decides the sex.

o.t: Whether the sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome
The mother, because the baby grows inside her
o.m: Believed the mother decides the sex, but all her eggs carry only X

o.t: Whether the egg carries an X or a Y chromosome
o.m: Thought the egg can carry either type, but all eggs carry only an X chromosome

o.t: The food the mother eats during pregnancy
o.m: Believed diet decides the sex, but it is fixed at fertilisation by the sperm

qs.q: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). What do the F1 plants look like?
qs.why: Tallness is dominant. Every F1 plant is Tt, so all of them are tall.

o.m: Mixed up the dominant and recessive trait

o.t: Half are tall and half are dwarf
o.m: Thought the two traits are shared equally in F1 instead of the dominant one showing
Believed the traits blend together, but Mendel found no blending

qs.q: The wings of a bird and the wings of an insect are used for flying but have a different origin and structure. What are such organs called?
qs.why: Organs with similar functions but different structure and origin are analogous organs.

o.m: Mixed up with organs of the same basic structure but different function, like human arm and bat wing
Mixed up with organs that have lost their function over time, like the appendix
Used a term that does not describe organs with similar function

qs.q: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt) are crossed and give 800 offspring. How many dwarf plants are expected?
qs.why: The ratio of tall to dwarf is 3 : 1, so 1/4 of the plants are dwarf: 800 ÷ 4 = 200.

o.m: Thought half the plants would be dwarf
Gave the number of tall plants instead of dwarf plants
Divided the total by 8 instead of by 4

qs.q: In a dihybrid cross of round yellow (RRYY) and wrinkled green (rryy) seeds, the F1 plants are crossed. Out of 16 F2 plants, how many are expected to be round and yellow?
qs.why: The F2 ratio is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, and the 9 are round yellow, which show both dominant traits.

o.m: Gave the number for one of the two mixed groups, round green or wrinkled yellow
Counted all round seeds, which includes the round green ones
Gave the number of wrinkled green plants, the double recessive

qs.q: When an antibiotic is used again and again, resistant bacteria become common. Which explanation is correct?
qs.why: A few bacteria already carried a variation for resistance. They survived and multiplied, so natural selection made them more common.

o.t: A few bacteria already had a variation that helped them survive and so they multiplied
Bacteria decided to become resistant when they met the antibiotic
o.m: Thought organisms change on purpose when needed, but variations arise by chance

o.t: The antibiotic turns every bacterium into a resistant one
o.m: Thought the medicine causes the same change in all bacteria instead of selecting existing variants

o.t: All bacteria were resistant from the start
o.m: Ignored variation; if all were resistant, the antibiotic would never have worked

s6_mat.name: Sorting materials and their properties
s6_mat.hi: पदार्थों का वर्गीकरण और उनके गुण

lesson.title: Sorting materials by their properties
points: We sort materials into groups by their properties, such as shine, hardness, solubility in water, floating or sinking, and transparency.
Metals have a shiny surface, which is called lustre. Iron and stone are hard, while cotton and sponge are soft.

Transparent materials (clear glass, air) let us see clearly through them. Translucent materials (butter paper) let only some light pass. Opaque materials (wood, metal, cardboard) do not let light pass.
Salt and sugar dissolve in water, so they are soluble. Sand and chalk powder do not dissolve, so they are insoluble. A cork floats on water, but an iron nail sinks.
lesson.story: In Amma's kitchen, the steel glass shines, sugar vanishes in the tea, a stone in the rice sinks in the water and the steel plate hides what is behind it. She is sorting materials by their properties without even knowing it.

example.q: Sort salt, sand, sugar and chalk powder into soluble and insoluble in water.
steps: Take four glasses of water and add one spoonful of each substance to its own glass.
Stir each glass well and wait for a minute. Salt and sugar disappear, because they dissolve in water.
Sand and chalk powder remain as particles and settle down. So salt and sugar are soluble; sand and chalk powder are insoluble.

qs.q: Which of these is a transparent material?
qs.why: Clear window glass lets us see clearly through it, so it is transparent.

o.m: Thought any thin, flat sheet lets us see through it.
Confused translucent with transparent, since some light passes through butter paper but objects look blurred.
Mixed up opaque with transparent.

qs.q: The shine on the surface of metals such as silver and copper is called:
qs.why: The shining surface of metals is called lustre.

o.m: Mixed up shine with dissolving in water.
Thought the property of blocking light is the same as shine.
Thought a shiny surface always means a hard material.

qs.q: Which pair of substances will both dissolve in water?
qs.why: Salt and sugar are both soluble in water, whereas sand and chalk powder are not.

o.m: Thought sand dissolves in water just like salt does.
Thought a fine powder always dissolves in water.
Thought any solid made of tiny grains disappears when stirred in water.

qs.q: Which of these will sink when dropped in water?
qs.why: An iron nail is heavy for its size and sinks, while cork, a dry leaf and thermocol float.

o.m: Thought every solid object sinks in water.
Thought a thin, light object soaks up water and sinks at once.
Thought a hard, solid-looking piece sinks like a stone.

qs.q: A sheet of butter paper is placed over a printed page and the letters look blurred but can still be seen. Butter paper is:
qs.why: Butter paper lets only some light pass through it, so objects look blurred. Such a material is translucent.

o.m: Thought that seeing anything at all through a material makes it transparent.
Thought that blurred vision means no light passes through.
Mixed up a property of a material with a source of light that gives out its own light.

qs.q: Which pair correctly classifies frosted glass (as in a bathroom window) and a wooden door?
qs.why: Frosted glass lets some light through but we cannot see clearly, so it is translucent. Wood blocks light, so it is opaque.

o.t: Frosted glass is transparent, wooden door is opaque
o.m: Thought that glass is always transparent whatever its surface is like.

o.t: Frosted glass is translucent, wooden door is opaque
Frosted glass is opaque, wooden door is translucent

qs.q: Meena stirs a spoonful of sand and a spoonful of sugar in a glass of water. What will she see after some time?
qs.why: Sugar is soluble and disappears into the water. Sand is insoluble and settles at the bottom.

o.m: Thought all tiny grains dissolve when stirred.
Thought solids always stay as grains in water.

o.t: Sugar disappears, sand settles at the bottom
Sand disappears, sugar settles at the bottom
o.m: Reversed which of the two substances is soluble.

qs.q: A school wants a classroom window that lets in daylight but does not let people outside see clearly into the room. Which material is best?
qs.why: Frosted (translucent) glass lets light in but blurs the view, so it gives light and privacy.

o.m: Forgot that transparent glass lets people outside see everything clearly.
Thought a shiny metal sheet lets light pass through.
