s6_food.name: Food: where it comes from and what it contains
s6_food.te: ఆహారం: ఆహార వనరులు మరియు ఆహార అనుఘటకాలు
s6_food.hi: भोजन: भोजन के स्रोत और भोजन के घटक

lesson.title: Food: where it comes from and what it contains
points: All our food comes from plants and animals. We eat roots (carrot), stems (sugarcane), leaves (spinach), flowers (cauliflower), fruits and seeds. Animals give milk, eggs and meat, and bees make honey from nectar.
Herbivores eat only plants (cow, goat), carnivores eat only animals (lion, tiger) and omnivores eat both (humans, crows).
Food contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. Carbohydrates and fats give energy, proteins help growth and repair, and vitamins and minerals protect the body from disease.

Lack of a nutrient causes a deficiency disease, such as scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D), anaemia (iron) and goitre (iodine). A balanced diet has all nutrients in the right amounts, along with roughage and water.
lesson.story: A thali is like a cricket team. Roti and rice are the big hitters who give energy, dal and curd build the body, and vegetables and fruits are the fielders who protect it. A team with only batsmen cannot win.

example.q: How can you test whether a slice of potato contains starch?
steps: Cut a thin slice of potato and place it on a plate.
Put 2 to 3 drops of dilute iodine solution on it.
The slice turns blue-black. This colour change shows that starch is present.

qs.q: Honey is made by bees from:
qs.why: Bees collect nectar from flowers and convert it into honey.

o.m: Thought bees collect the honey from leaves.
Thought bees make honey out of ordinary sugar.
Thought bees gather ready-made honey from ripe fruits.

qs.q: Animals that eat both plants and animals are called:
qs.why: Omnivores eat both plants and animals. Humans and crows are omnivores.

o.m: Thought animals that eat some plants feed only on plants.
Thought any animal that eats meat eats only meat.
Mixed up a feeding group with organisms that break down dead matter.

qs.q: Which nutrient mainly helps in the growth and repair of the body?
qs.why: Proteins build new cells and repair worn-out ones, so they are called body-building nutrients.

o.m: Thought the main energy-giving food also builds the body.
Thought a food that stores energy also repairs the body.
Thought vitamins build muscles because they are essential.

qs.q: A drop of iodine solution turns blue-black when put on a food item. The item contains:
qs.why: Iodine solution turns blue-black in the presence of starch.

o.m: Mixed up the iodine test with the copper sulphate and caustic soda test for proteins.
Mixed up the iodine test with the oil-stain test done on paper.
Thought iodine solution detects vitamins.

qs.q: Which of these is a root that we eat as a vegetable?
qs.why: A carrot is the root of the carrot plant. Cauliflower is a flower, spinach is a leaf and potato is a stem.

o.m: Thought anything that grows under the soil must be a root.
Thought a vegetable with a white, bulky head is a root.
Thought all green vegetables come from the roots.

qs.q: Ravi ate only polished rice, with no fruits or vegetables, for months. His gums began to bleed. He most likely lacks:
qs.why: Bleeding gums are a sign of scurvy, which is caused by lack of vitamin C. Fruits and vegetables like amla and lemon give vitamin C.

o.m: Linked weakness of the body with the vitamin got from sunlight, which affects bones.
Linked a problem of the throat and neck with the body's tissues.
Linked blood-related problems with bleeding gums.

qs.q: Neha's meals are mostly rice and potato curry. To add mainly proteins to her diet, she should add:
qs.why: Dal, milk, eggs and fish are rich in proteins. Rice and potato mostly give carbohydrates.

o.m: Thought sweet foods give body-building nutrients.
Thought more of the same energy food would supply proteins.
Thought a rich, heavy food builds the body.

qs.q: Sunita looks pale and feels tired all the time. The doctor says she has anaemia and advises spinach and jaggery. Which nutrient is she lacking?
qs.why: Anaemia is caused by lack of iron, and spinach and jaggery are good sources of iron.

o.m: Linked tiredness with weak bones and teeth.
Linked her illness with the swelling of the neck.
Linked her illness with eyesight problems.

lesson.title: Separating the useful from the unwanted
points: Most things around us are mixtures. We separate the useful part from the non-useful part by handpicking, threshing, winnowing and sieving.
In winnowing, wind blows away the lighter husk while the heavier grain falls down. Sieving separates particles of different sizes.

Insoluble solids settle at the bottom in sedimentation, and the clear liquid is poured out in decantation. Filtration with filter paper or cloth removes fine insoluble particles. Evaporation gets a dissolved solid (like salt) from its solution.
When no more solute dissolves in a solution at a given temperature, it is a saturated solution. Heating the water lets it dissolve more.
lesson.story: Amma first picks stones out of rice, then washes it in a vessel, lets it settle and pours the dirty water out. At the sea coast, people fill shallow pans with sea water and let the Sun dry it to get salt.

example.q: How can you get back both the sand and the salt from a mixture of the two?
steps: Add water to the mixture and stir well. The salt dissolves but the sand does not.
Filter the mixture. The sand stays on the filter paper and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate.
Heat the filtrate so that the water evaporates. The salt is left behind in the dish.

qs.q: Separating husk from grain by blowing wind over the mixture is called:
qs.why: In winnowing, the lighter husk is blown away by wind and the heavier grain falls down.

o.m: Mixed up the two farm methods, since threshing frees the grains from the stalks.
Thought wind is used with a sieve.
Thought the husk is removed by picking it up by hand.

qs.q: Which method is used to get salt from sea water?
qs.why: When sea water is left in shallow pans, the water evaporates and the salt is left behind.

o.m: Thought wind separates a dissolved solid from a liquid.
Forgot that salt is dissolved in water and cannot settle down to be poured off.
Thought a sieve can hold back the dissolved salt.

qs.q: Muddy pond water is left to stand for some time and the clear water is then gently poured out. These two steps are called:
qs.why: Heavier particles settling at the bottom is sedimentation. Pouring out the clear water is decantation.

o.m: Thought removing the dirt needs the water to be turned into vapour.
Mixed up farm methods with methods of separating a solid from a liquid.
Thought a filter is needed even though the dirt settles on its own.

qs.q: Which method separates a mixture of fine sand and small stones of different sizes?
qs.why: A sieve lets the fine sand pass through and holds back the bigger stones.

o.m: Thought heating is needed to separate two dry solids.
Mixed up a change of state with separating particles by size.
Thought pouring is enough, though no liquid is present.

qs.q: Which of these mixtures can be separated by filtering through a clean cloth?
qs.why: Chalk powder does not dissolve, so its fine particles are caught by the cloth. Dissolved salt and sugar pass through the cloth.

o.m: Thought dissolved salt gets caught in the cloth.
Thought a dissolved solid stays as particles that a filter can hold back.
Thought two liquids that mix can be separated by a filter.

qs.q: What is the correct way to get both sand and salt back from a dry mixture of the two?
qs.why: Water dissolves the salt but not the sand. Filtering removes the sand, and evaporating the filtrate leaves the salt.

o.t: Heat the dry mixture and then filter it
o.m: Thought heating separates two dry solids and then a filter can be used.

o.t: Add water, evaporate everything, then filter
o.m: Evaporated before removing the sand, so the sand and salt were mixed again.

o.t: Winnow the mixture and then sieve it
o.m: Thought wind can separate two heavy solids of similar weight.

o.t: Add water, filter, then evaporate the filtrate

qs.q: A farmer harvests wheat. In which order does he separate the grains from the stalks and then the husk from the grains?
qs.why: First threshing frees the grains from the stalks, and then winnowing blows away the lighter husk.

o.m: Reversed the order, although husk cannot be separated before grains are freed from the stalks.
Thought a sieve is the first step on the harvested crop.
Thought evaporation is used for dry grains.

qs.q: Rani keeps adding salt to water in a glass and stirring. After some time, some salt remains at the bottom even after stirring well. The solution is:
qs.why: When no more salt can dissolve at that temperature, the solution is saturated.

o.m: Thought a solution with salt at the bottom can still dissolve more at the same temperature.
Thought that undissolved salt at the bottom means salt is not soluble at all.
Mixed up condensation (vapour turning to liquid) with a strong solution.

lesson.title: Parts of a plant and what they do
points: Plants are of three kinds. Herbs are small with green, tender stems. Shrubs have hard but not very thick stems that branch near the base. Trees are tall with a thick, hard trunk. Climbers and creepers have weak stems.
Roots hold the plant in the soil and absorb water and minerals. A tap root has one main root with side roots (mustard, carrot). Fibrous roots are a cluster of thin roots (wheat, grass).
The stem carries water and minerals up to the leaves and carries food to other parts. Leaves make food by photosynthesis and give out water vapour through tiny pores called stomata.

A flower has sepals, petals, stamens (male part) and a pistil (female part). Leaves with net-like veins usually belong to plants with tap roots, and leaves with parallel veins to plants with fibrous roots.
lesson.story: A plant is like a house with a borewell. The roots are the borewell, the stem is the pipe that lifts the water, and the leaves are the kitchen where the food is cooked.

example.q: A plant has leaves with a net-like pattern of veins. What kind of root does it most likely have, and how can you tell?
steps: Look at the veins of the leaf. A net-like pattern is called reticulate venation.
Plants with reticulate venation generally have a tap root, with one main root and many side roots, like a mustard plant.
Plants with parallel veins (grass, wheat) generally have fibrous roots instead.

qs.q: Which part of a plant absorbs water and minerals from the soil?
qs.why: The roots absorb water and minerals from the soil and also hold the plant firmly.

o.m: Thought the stem, which carries water upwards, is also what takes water from the soil.
Thought the leaves drink water as the plant's mouth.
Thought flowers take in water for forming fruits.

qs.q: The tiny pores on the surface of leaves, through which water vapour escapes, are called:
qs.why: Stomata are tiny pores on leaves. Water vapour leaves through them in transpiration.

o.m: Thought the lines on a leaf are what let out the water vapour.
Mixed up the leaf stalk with the pores on the leaf.
Mixed up a part of the flower with a part of the leaf.

qs.q: Which of these plants has fibrous roots?
qs.why: Wheat has fibrous roots, a cluster of thin roots of similar size. Mustard, carrot and gram have tap roots.

o.m: Thought all crop plants have a single main root.
Thought a thick edible root means a fibrous root system.
Thought all plants that give seeds have fibrous roots.

qs.q: A pea plant has a weak stem and climbs up a fence using tendrils. It is called a:
qs.why: Plants with weak stems that climb up a support are called climbers.

o.m: Thought all weak-stemmed plants are creepers, though creepers spread along the ground.
Thought any small plant with branches is a shrub.
Thought a plant that goes up high must be a tree.

qs.q: Which part of a flower is the male part?
qs.why: The stamen produces pollen and is the male part of the flower. The pistil is the female part.

o.m: Mixed up the male and female parts of a flower.
Thought the colourful part makes the pollen.
Thought the green outer part makes the pollen.

qs.q: A celery stalk is kept in water coloured with red ink. After some hours, red lines can be seen inside the stem and in the leaves. This shows that the stem:
qs.why: The coloured water rises through the stem to the leaves, which shows that the stem carries water upwards.

o.t: Carries water up to the leaves

o.m: Thought the colour in the stem means the stem is storing something, like food.
Thought the stem is the part that cooks the food.
Mixed up the work of the stem with the work of the roots.

qs.q: A leafy branch is covered with a clear polythene bag and tied. After some hours, drops of water collect inside the bag. This shows that leaves:
qs.why: Leaves give out water vapour through stomata (transpiration). The vapour cools and forms drops on the bag.

o.t: Absorb water vapour from the air
o.m: Thought the water drops show that the leaves take in water from the air.
Thought the drops are caused by carbon dioxide.
Thought the drops are a product of food-making.

qs.q: A student finds that a leaf has parallel veins. Which root system does the plant most likely have?
qs.why: Plants whose leaves have parallel veins (grass, maize) generally have fibrous roots.

o.m: Reversed the link, since tap roots go with net-like veins.

o.t: Roots that grow only in the air
o.m: Mixed up with plants like banyan that have roots growing in the air.
Thought a plant with narrow leaves does not need roots.

lesson.title: Measuring length and describing motion
points: Earlier people used a cubit, handspan, foot or pace to measure length. These differ from person to person, so we use standard units. The SI unit of length is the metre (m). 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm and 1 km = 1000 m.

While measuring with a scale, place the object along it with one end at the zero mark, or note the other mark and subtract. Keep the eye directly above the mark being read. A curved line is measured with a thread, which is then straightened and measured.
Motion can be in a straight line (rectilinear), along a circle (circular), spinning about a fixed point (rotational) or to and fro again and again (periodic or oscillatory).
Whether an object is at rest or in motion depends on what we compare it with. A person sitting in a moving bus is at rest with respect to the bus but moving with respect to the trees outside.
lesson.story: If the cloth seller at the market measured your kurta cloth with his own handspan, you and your neighbour would get different lengths for the same price. That is why every shop uses a metre tape.

example.q: A road is 2.5 km long. Express its length in metres and in centimetres.
steps: The road is 2500 m or 250000 cm long.

qs.q: The SI unit of length is the:
qs.why: The SI unit of length is the metre.

o.m: Took a smaller, commonly used unit to be the SI unit.
Took the unit used for road distances as the SI unit.
Used a non-SI unit that people use in daily life.

qs.q: A child sitting on a swing moves to and fro again and again. This is an example of:
qs.why: The motion of a swing repeats after a fixed time, so it is a periodic (oscillatory) motion.

o.m: Thought a path that goes both ways is a straight line.
Thought any curved path is a circular motion.
Thought the swing is spinning about a fixed point like a top.

qs.q: How many centimetres are there in 4.5 m?

o.m: Divided or multiplied by 10 instead of 100.
Multiplied by 1000 instead of 100.
Divided by 100 instead of multiplying.

qs.q: While reading the length of a pencil on a ruler, where should the eye be?
qs.why: The eye should be directly above the mark being read, looking straight down, to avoid a wrong reading.

o.t: A little to the left of the mark
o.m: Thought the angle of the eye does not change the reading.

o.t: A little to the right of the mark
o.m: Thought looking from the side gives a more clear view.

o.t: Anywhere, as the reading is always the same
o.m: Thought the position of the eye never matters.

o.t: Directly above the mark, looking straight down

qs.q: Which of these is an example of rotational motion?
qs.why: The blades of a ceiling fan spin about a fixed point, which is rotational motion.

o.t: A car moving on a straight road
o.m: Mixed up straight-line motion with spinning about a point.

o.t: Blades of a ceiling fan turning

o.m: Thought any motion that goes quickly is rotation.

o.t: A pendulum swinging to and fro
o.m: Thought any repeating motion is rotation.

qs.q: Ravi wants to find the length of a curved path drawn on a map. Which is the best method?
qs.why: A thread laid along the curve can be straightened and measured on a ruler, which gives the length of the curved path.

o.t: Place a ruler straight between the two ends
o.m: Measured only the straight-line distance between ends and not the curve.

o.t: Count the number of handspans along the curve
o.m: Used a non-standard unit that differs from person to person.

o.t: Lay a thread along the curve, then straighten it and measure it on a ruler
Measure the paper's edge with a ruler
o.m: Thought the length of the path is the same as the size of the map.

qs.q: The zero end of a ruler is broken. A book's one end is at the 2.0 cm mark and the other end is at the 17.5 cm mark. What is the length of the book?
qs.why: Length = 17.5 cm − 2.0 cm = 15.5 cm.

o.m: Read only the second end and ignored the starting mark.
Added the two readings instead of subtracting them.
Made a mistake in subtracting the two readings.

qs.q: A passenger sits in a bus moving steadily along a straight road. Which statement is correct?
qs.why: The passenger does not change position with respect to the bus, so is at rest with respect to it. With respect to a tree outside, the passenger's position changes, so is in motion.

o.t: At rest with respect to the tree but moving with respect to the bus
o.m: Reversed the two reference points.

o.t: At rest with respect to the bus but moving with respect to a tree
Always at rest, since the passenger is not moving the body
o.m: Thought that rest or motion does not depend on what we compare with.

o.t: Moving with respect to the bus but also with respect to the tree
o.m: Thought that the passenger moves with respect to the seat as well.

lesson.title: Light, shadows and reflection
points: Objects that give out light of their own, like the Sun, stars, a lamp or a candle flame, are luminous. The Moon, a table or a book is non-luminous. We see them when light from a source falls on them and reaches our eyes.
Light travels in straight lines. An opaque object in its path stops the light and a shadow forms on a screen behind it. A shadow needs a source of light, an opaque object and a screen.
The nearer an object is to the source of light, the bigger its shadow. A pinhole camera forms an upside-down (inverted) image.
A mirror reflects light. The image in a plane mirror is the same size as the object, and left and right appear interchanged.
lesson.story: During a power cut, children make shadow puppets on the wall with a lamp. When the hand is moved close to the lamp, the shadow becomes huge, and when it is moved close to the wall it shrinks.

example.q: We can see the Moon at night although it has no light of its own. Explain how.
steps: The Moon is non-luminous. It does not make its own light.
The Sun is luminous. Sunlight falls on the Moon and is reflected by its surface.
This reflected light travels to our eyes and so we see the Moon.

qs.q: Which of these is a luminous object?
qs.why: A burning candle gives out its own light, so it is luminous. The Moon and a mirror only reflect light.

o.m: Thought that anything bright in the sky makes its own light.
Thought shiny things shine on their own.
Thought that a brightly lit object is a source of light.

qs.q: Light travels in:
qs.why: Light travels in straight lines. That is why we get shadows with sharp edges.

o.m: Thought light bends round corners to reach us.
Thought light changes direction on its own.
Thought light goes around objects in circles.

qs.q: Which three things are needed to form a shadow?
qs.why: A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks the light from a source and falls on a screen.

o.t: A source of light, a transparent object and a screen
o.m: Thought a transparent object blocks the light.

o.t: A source of light, an opaque object and a screen
A mirror, an opaque object and a screen
o.m: Thought a shadow is formed by reflection from a mirror.

o.t: An opaque object and a screen only
o.m: Forgot that a source of light is needed.

qs.q: The image formed in a pinhole camera is:
qs.why: Light travels in straight lines through the pinhole, so the top of the object forms the bottom of the image. The image is inverted.

o.m: Thought the image is like the one seen in a mirror.

o.t: Absent, as the hole is too small
o.m: Thought a tiny hole cannot let enough light in to form an image.

o.t: Upright and larger than the object
o.m: Thought a camera always makes the image bigger.

qs.q: Which statement about the image in a plane mirror is correct?
qs.why: The image in a plane mirror is the same size as the object, with left and right sides interchanged.

o.t: Same size as the object, with left and right interchanged
Smaller than the object, but upright
o.m: Thought the image is smaller because it seems to be farther away.

o.t: Larger than the object and upside down
o.m: Mixed up a plane mirror with a pinhole camera.

o.t: Same size as the object, with top and bottom interchanged
o.m: Thought the image is turned upside down and not sideways.

qs.q: Why can we see the Moon at night, although it is non-luminous?
qs.why: The Moon reflects sunlight, and this light reaches our eyes.

o.t: It makes its own light like a star
o.m: Thought that the Moon is a luminous object.

o.t: It reflects the light of the Sun towards us
It is lit by the light of stars
o.m: Thought starlight is what makes the Moon bright.

o.t: It absorbs the Sun's light and glows in the dark
o.m: Thought the Moon stores sunlight during the day and gives it out at night.

qs.q: A ball is held between a lamp and a wall near the lamp. Rani slowly moves the ball towards the wall. What happens to the shadow of the ball on the wall?
qs.why: The nearer the object is to the light source, the bigger the shadow. So as the ball moves away from the lamp, the shadow becomes smaller.

o.m: Thought that moving an object towards the screen makes its shadow larger.
Thought the shadow size depends only on the size of the ball.

o.t: It disappears when the ball nears the wall
o.m: Thought that shadows form only in the space between the object and screen.

qs.q: The word AMBULANCE is written laterally inverted (reversed) on the front of the vehicle. Why?
qs.why: A driver ahead sees the reflection in the rear-view mirror, where left and right are interchanged again, so the word can be read correctly.

o.t: So that drivers ahead can read it properly in their rear-view mirrors
So that the letters look bigger
o.m: Thought that reversed letters take more space.

o.t: So that more light is reflected from it
o.m: Thought that reversed letters reflect more light.
Thought the reversal has no real purpose.

lesson.title: Electricity and circuits
points: An electric cell is a source of electricity. It has two terminals, a positive terminal (metal cap) and a negative terminal (metal disc). A battery is a combination of two or more cells.

A bulb has a thin filament between its two terminals, and the filament glows when electricity passes through it. A bulb glows only when the circuit is closed, that is, a complete path joins the two terminals of the cell through the bulb.
A switch opens or closes the circuit. In the OFF position there is a gap, so the current cannot flow.

Conductors let electricity pass through them (metals like copper and iron). Insulators do not (plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass). We should never use mains electricity for experiments and never touch switches with wet hands.
lesson.story: A circuit is like the round track in a school relay race. If the track is complete, the baton goes from runner to runner and back to the start. If there is a gap anywhere, the race stops.

example.q: A bulb is joined to a cell by wires and a switch, but it does not glow even when the switch is ON. Give possible reasons.
steps: The filament of the bulb may be broken (a fused bulb), so the path inside the bulb is not complete.
A wire may be loose or may not be touching a terminal, leaving a gap in the circuit.
The cell may have run out of its chemicals, so it cannot push the electricity through the circuit.

qs.q: Which of these is a good conductor of electricity?
qs.why: Copper is a metal, and metals are good conductors of electricity. Rubber, dry wood and plastic are insulators.

o.m: Thought a soft, flexible material carries current.
Thought a long, straight stick can carry current.
Saw plastic around electric wires and thought plastic carries the current.

qs.q: The metal cap of an electric cell is its:
qs.why: The metal cap of a cell is its positive terminal. The metal disc at the other end is the negative terminal.

o.m: Mixed up the two terminals of the cell.
Mixed up a part of a cell with a part of a bulb.
Thought the metal cap turns the cell on and off.

qs.q: A bulb will glow only when:
qs.why: A bulb glows when there is a complete closed path from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, to the other terminal.

o.t: One wire joins the bulb to one terminal of the cell
o.m: Thought one wire is enough for the bulb to glow.

o.t: A complete closed path joins the two cell terminals through the bulb
The switch is in the OFF position
o.m: Thought an open switch lets the current pass.

o.t: The bulb is kept far from the cell
o.m: Thought the bulb gets electricity without any connection.

qs.q: A bulb, a cell and a switch are joined correctly and the switch is ON, but the bulb does not glow. Which is the most likely reason?
qs.why: If the filament is broken, there is a gap in the circuit and the bulb will not glow.

o.t: The switch is in the ON position
o.m: Thought that a closed switch stops the current.

o.t: The wires have a plastic covering
o.m: Forgot that the covering is only outside, while the metal inside conducts.
Thought that a cell with two terminals cannot light a bulb.

o.t: The filament of the bulb is broken

qs.q: Which set contains only insulators?
qs.why: A plastic comb, a rubber band and a dry wooden stick are all poor conductors, so they are insulators.

o.t: Plastic comb, rubber band, dry wooden stick

o.m: Counted a metal as an insulator since it is solid and hard.
Thought a shiny coin does not let current pass.
Counted a thin metal sheet as an insulator.

qs.q: An electrician uses a screwdriver with a plastic handle when repairing a switch. Why?
qs.why: Plastic is an insulator, so it does not let current pass to the electrician's hand, which protects from an electric shock.

o.t: Plastic is a conductor and carries the current away
o.m: Thought a conductor in the handle makes it safe.
Thought the handle is only for appearance.

o.t: Plastic is an insulator and protects from electric shock

o.m: Thought that more weight makes the tool safer.

qs.q: A student replaces a piece of copper wire in a working circuit with a dry cotton thread. The bulb stops glowing. Why?
qs.why: Dry cotton thread is an insulator, so it does not allow the electric current to pass and the circuit is not complete.

o.t: The thread is conducting but is too long
o.m: Thought that a conductor with some length stops the current.

o.t: The thread is thinner, so the bulb became dim and then went off
o.m: Thought a thread conducts a little and then fails.

o.t: The thread gets burnt by the current
o.m: Thought the thread was burnt because the current passed through it.

o.t: Dry cotton thread is an insulator and breaks the path of the current

qs.q: Why does a bulb not glow when the switch is in the OFF position?
qs.why: In the OFF position the switch leaves a gap in the circuit, so the path for the current is broken.

o.t: The switch takes out the chemicals of the cell
o.m: Thought the switch changes something inside the cell.

o.t: The switch leaves a gap and the circuit is broken
The switch turns the wires into insulators
o.m: Thought the switch changes the material of the wire.

o.t: The switch removes the filament from the bulb
o.m: Thought the switch changes something inside the bulb.

lesson.title: How living things get food
points: Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are called autotrophs.
In photosynthesis, chlorophyll in the leaf uses sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make carbohydrate (food) and releases oxygen.
Animals cannot make food, so they depend on plants or other animals. Some plants are parasites, saprotrophs or live in symbiosis.
In humans, food moves from mouth to food pipe, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. Digestion is completed and food is absorbed in the small intestine.
lesson.story: A leaf is a small kitchen. Sunlight is the gas stove, water and carbon dioxide are the ingredients, and chlorophyll is the cook who prepares food for the whole plant.

example.q: Name the raw materials and the products of photosynthesis.
steps: Raw materials: carbon dioxide (entering through stomata on the leaf) and water (taken in by the roots).
Energy: sunlight, which is trapped by chlorophyll in the green leaf.
Products: food in the form of carbohydrate (stored as starch) and oxygen, which goes out into the air.

qs.q: Which green pigment in leaves traps sunlight for photosynthesis?
qs.why: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in leaves that traps the energy of sunlight.

o.m: Confused it with the red pigment found in blood.
Mixed up a pigment with the tiny pores on a leaf.
Thought the material of plant cell walls was the pigment.

qs.q: In humans, digestion is completed and digested food is absorbed in the:
qs.why: Digestion is completed in the small intestine, and its inner walls (villi) absorb the digested food into the blood.

o.m: Thought the stomach, which churns food, also absorbs it.
Mixed up absorption of food with absorption of water in the large intestine.
Thought the food pipe digests food while passing it down.

qs.q: Amarbel (Cuscuta) is a yellow, leafless climber that takes ready-made food from the plant it grows on. It is a:
qs.why: Cuscuta lacks chlorophyll and feeds on its host plant, so it is a parasite.

o.m: Thought it feeds on dead and decaying matter like fungi do.
Thought every plant makes its own food.
Mixed it up with the pitcher plant, which traps insects.

qs.q: Meena chews a piece of plain chapati for a few minutes and it begins to taste sweet. Why?
qs.why: Saliva in the mouth turns starch of the chapati into sugar, which tastes sweet.

o.t: The teeth change the starch into sugar by grinding it
o.m: Thought chewing alone (mechanical action) changes starch into sugar.

o.t: Chapati contains sugar that was added while cooking
o.m: Assumed sugar was already present and ignored what saliva does.

o.t: Saliva changes the starch in chapati into sugar
Saliva changes the proteins in chapati into starch
o.m: Reversed the change and mixed up which nutrient saliva acts on.

qs.q: Through which tiny pores on a leaf does carbon dioxide enter for photosynthesis?
qs.why: Stomata are tiny pores on the leaf surface through which carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves.

o.m: Thought roots take in all raw materials, including gases.
Thought the veins, which carry water, are the openings for air.
Thought the flower takes in the gas for making food.

qs.q: Rhizobium bacteria live in the root nodules of pea plants and give them nitrogen. The plant gives the bacteria food and shelter. This relationship is called:
qs.why: When two organisms live together and both benefit, it is called symbiosis.

o.m: Thought living inside a plant always harms the plant.
Thought bacteria always feed on dead and rotting matter.
Thought any organism that takes in food is holozoic, ignoring that this is animal-type feeding.

qs.q: A leaf from a plant kept in a dark cupboard for several days is boiled and tested with iodine solution. What is seen and why?
qs.why: Without sunlight there is no photosynthesis, so no starch is made, and iodine does not turn blue-black.

o.t: Blue-black, because chlorophyll can make starch even without light
o.m: Thought chlorophyll makes food without sunlight.

o.t: Blue-black, because iodine itself turns sugar into starch
o.m: Thought iodine produces starch instead of only detecting it.

o.t: No blue-black colour, because without light no photosynthesis and no starch
No blue-black colour, because starch is made only at night
o.m: Mixed up day and night, thinking photosynthesis happens in the dark.

qs.q: A cow swallows grass quickly and later brings it back to the mouth to chew. Why?
qs.why: Ruminants like cows store swallowed grass in the rumen, where it is partly digested; they then chew this cud again so that cellulose-rich grass is digested well.

o.t: The partly digested food (cud) is chewed again so the cellulose-rich grass can be digested
The first chewing leaves waste, which the cow chews and passes out as cud
o.m: Thought cud is waste material.

o.t: The cow makes milk from the cud, so it has to chew it again
o.m: Thought chewing cud is how milk is made.

o.t: Grass is not swallowed at all; the cow only tastes it before spitting it out
o.m: Ignored that the cow swallows grass and stores it in the rumen.

lesson.title: Hot, cold and how heat travels
points: Temperature tells us how hot or cold a thing is. It is measured with a thermometer in degrees Celsius (°C).
A clinical thermometer measures body temperature and reads from 35°C to 42°C. Normal human body temperature is about 37°C. A laboratory thermometer reads from −10°C to 110°C.
Heat flows from a hotter to a colder place. In solids it moves by conduction, in liquids and gases by convection, and the Sun's heat reaches us by radiation, which needs no medium.
Dark colours absorb more heat and light colours reflect more heat. Wool is a poor conductor and traps air, so it keeps us warm.
lesson.story: A steel spoon left in hot sabzi soon becomes too hot to hold, but the wooden handle of the ladle stays comfortable. Heat travels easily along metal but not along wood.

example.q: Why do we wear light-coloured cotton clothes in a hot summer but dark woollen clothes in winter?
steps: In summer the Sun's heat is strong. Light colours reflect most of it, so we feel cooler.
In winter dark colours absorb more heat and help us feel warmer.
Wool is a poor conductor of heat and traps air in it, so body heat does not escape easily.

qs.q: The normal temperature of a healthy human body is about:
qs.why: The normal body temperature is about 37°C, which lies in the 35°C to 42°C range of a clinical thermometer.

o.m: Took the lowest mark of the clinical thermometer as the normal value.
Took the highest mark of the clinical thermometer as the normal value.
Used the Fahrenheit value of 98.6 but wrote it as degrees Celsius.

qs.q: A clinical thermometer is used to measure the human body temperature. Its scale ranges from:
qs.why: A clinical thermometer reads from 35°C to 42°C, because human body temperature lies within this range.

o.m: Gave the range of a laboratory thermometer.
Thought it covers the freezing and boiling points of water.
Guessed a range without linking it to body temperature.

qs.q: A steel spoon kept in a pan of hot dal becomes hot at the other end too. Heat reaches the handle mainly by:
qs.why: In solids, especially metals, heat travels from the hot part to the cooler part by conduction.

o.m: Thought particles of the metal move along the spoon, as in liquids.
Thought the spoon gets heat only as waves without touching the dal.
Mixed up heat transfer with a change of state of the dal.

qs.q: Why is it better to wear light-coloured clothes in summer?
qs.why: Light colours reflect more heat than dark colours, so less heat reaches the body.

o.t: Light colours absorb more heat and take it away from the body
o.m: Thought absorbing heat makes a surface cooler.

o.t: Light-coloured clothes are always made of thicker cloth
o.m: Linked colour with thickness of cloth instead of with heat reflection.

o.t: Light colours produce cold that cools the body
o.m: Thought colours can produce coldness by themselves.

o.t: Light colours reflect most of the heat falling on them

qs.q: The heat of the Sun reaches the Earth through the empty space by:
qs.why: Space has no air or matter, so heat comes to Earth by radiation, which needs no medium.

o.m: Thought heat always travels by touching particles, forgetting there is no matter in space.
Thought hot air currents carry heat all the way from the Sun.
Mixed up reflection of light with the way heat travels.

qs.q: On a hot afternoon, a cool breeze blows from the sea towards the land. Why?
qs.why: Land heats up faster than water. Air above the land becomes hot and rises, and cooler air from the sea moves in to take its place.

o.t: Air above the sea gets hotter than the land and rises, pulling air from the land
o.m: Reversed the roles of land and water in heating.

o.t: The sea sends out cold radiation which pushes the air towards the land
o.m: Thought the sea gives out cold as if it were a heat source.

o.t: Warm air over the land rises, and cooler air from the sea rushes in
Water vapour is lighter than the land, so it pushes the air inland
o.m: Confused moisture in the air with the cause of air movement.

qs.q: Water in a pan is heated only from the bottom, yet the whole water becomes hot. This mainly happens because:
qs.why: Heated water at the bottom becomes lighter and rises while cooler water from the top sinks, setting up convection currents.

o.t: Hot water rises and cooler water sinks, forming convection currents
Water is a good conductor, so heat passes quickly through each layer
o.m: Thought water conducts heat well; liquids are poor conductors.

o.t: Heat from the stove reaches the top of the water by radiation alone
o.m: Ignored the movement of water and gave radiation as the only reason.

o.t: The pan lid pushes the heat back down into the water
o.m: Thought the lid is the reason for heating the whole water.

qs.q: Rani feels warm in a woollen sweater on a cold morning in Shimla. The best reason is that:
qs.why: Wool is a poor conductor of heat and traps air between its fibres, so body heat does not easily escape.

o.t: Wool produces heat of its own and passes it to the body
o.m: Thought wool is a source of heat.

o.t: Wool traps air and is a poor conductor, so body heat stays in
Wool is a good conductor and brings outside warmth to the body
o.m: Mixed up good and poor conductors.

o.t: Wool absorbs the cold from outside and stores it away
o.m: Thought cold is a substance that clothes can soak up.

lesson.title: Acids, bases and salts
points: Acids taste sour, like lemon, tamarind and curd. Bases taste bitter and feel soapy, like baking soda and soap solution. We must never taste unknown substances.
Indicators show if a substance is acidic or basic. Acids turn blue litmus red and bases turn red litmus blue. Turmeric turns red with bases. China rose turns magenta with acids and green with bases.
A neutral substance, like pure water, does not change the colour of litmus.
When an acid and a base react, they cancel each other's effect. This is neutralisation, and it forms salt and water and gives out heat.
lesson.story: When a red ant bites, it leaves formic acid on your skin and it burns. Dadi puts a paste of baking soda on it. The mild base cancels the acid and the burning goes away.

example.q: Why is slaked lime spread on a farmer's field when the soil is too acidic?
steps: Excess acid in the soil is harmful for the growth of many plants.
Slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) is a base, so it reacts with the acid in the soil.
This is neutralisation. The acid is cancelled and the soil becomes suitable for crops again.

qs.q: A solution turns blue litmus paper red. The solution is:
qs.why: Acids turn blue litmus red, so the solution is acidic.

o.m: Mixed up the colour changes of acids and bases on litmus.
Thought any colour change on litmus means the solution is neutral.
Thought a colour change shows pure water, which does not change litmus.

qs.q: Which acid is present in curd?
qs.why: Curd contains lactic acid, which gives it a sour taste.

o.m: Mixed up with the acid in lemon and orange.
Mixed up with the acid in vinegar.
Mixed up with the acid in tamarind.

qs.q: A yellow turmeric paper dipped in soap solution turns red. This shows that soap solution is:
qs.why: Turmeric turns red only with bases, so soap solution is basic.

o.m: Thought turmeric turns red with acids, as red litmus does.
Thought a colour change on turmeric means a neutral solution.

o.t: An acid and a base at the same time
o.m: Thought one colour change can show both acid and base.

qs.q: A red ant bite leaves formic acid on the skin. What gives the most relief?
qs.why: Formic acid is neutralised by a mild base such as baking soda.

o.m: Thought another acid would remove the acid.
Thought a sour liquid would remove the acid.
Thought a neutral sweet liquid neutralises the acid.

qs.q: When hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, the products are:
qs.why: An acid and a base react to form salt and water. Here the salt is common salt.

o.m: Thought the acid and base only break into their elements.

o.t: A stronger acid and a stronger base
o.m: Thought mixing makes the two substances stronger instead of cancelling.
Forgot that a salt is formed along with water.

qs.q: A farmer finds that his field soil is too acidic. Which substance should he add to treat it?
qs.why: Acidic soil is neutralised by adding a base such as slaked lime or quicklime.

o.m: Thought a sour liquid would improve the soil.
Thought salt neutralises acids because it is called a salt.
Thought adding more acid would balance the soil.

qs.q: Why does a person with acidity (indigestion) take a tablet or syrup of milk of magnesia?
qs.why: Excess acid in the stomach causes indigestion. Milk of magnesia is a base that neutralises the excess acid.

o.t: It is an acid that helps digest more food
o.m: Thought adding acid helps cure too much acid.

o.t: It is a base and neutralises the excess acid in the stomach
It is a salt that dissolves the food in the stomach
o.m: Mixed up the role of a salt with that of an antacid.

o.t: It cools the stomach by absorbing the heat
o.m: Thought acidity is only an excess of heat.

qs.q: A drop of China rose solution turns green in liquid P and stays magenta (dark pink) in liquid Q. What can be concluded?
qs.why: China rose turns green with a base and magenta with an acid, so P is basic and Q is acidic.

o.t: P is acidic and Q is basic
o.m: Reversed the colours of China rose with acids and bases.

o.t: P is neutral and Q is acidic
o.m: Thought green means a neutral substance.

o.t: Both P and Q are basic
o.m: Thought any colour change in China rose means a base.

o.t: P is basic and Q is acidic

lesson.title: Physical and chemical changes
points: In a physical change, only properties like shape, size, colour or state change. No new substance forms, and it is often easy to reverse. Melting ice and dissolving sugar are examples.
In a chemical change, one or more new substances form with new properties. It is usually difficult to reverse. Burning, cooking, rusting and curdling of milk are examples.
Rusting needs both oxygen (air) and water. We prevent it by painting, greasing or coating iron with zinc (galvanisation).
Chemical changes can give out heat, light, gas, a new smell or a change of colour.
lesson.story: An ice gola melts in your hand and you can freeze it again: that is physical. But a roti cooked on a tawa can never become dough again: that is chemical.

example.q: Is rusting of an iron gate a physical or a chemical change? Give reasons.
steps: Iron reacts with oxygen and water in the air.
A new reddish-brown substance, rust (iron oxide), forms. It is not iron and has different properties.
We cannot get the iron back by simply reversing the change, so rusting is a chemical change.

qs.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
qs.why: Rusting forms a new substance, rust, so it is a chemical change.

o.m: Thought a change of state forms a new substance.
Thought a change in shape and size makes a new substance.
Thought that since sugar vanishes, a new substance must have formed.

qs.q: Which two things are needed for iron to rust?
qs.why: Rusting needs both oxygen (from air) and water (moisture).

o.m: Thought dry air alone can rust iron.
Thought water alone is enough, ignoring the air.
Mixed up rusting with the needs of photosynthesis.

qs.q: Milk kept overnight in a warm kitchen becomes curd. Why is this a chemical change?
qs.why: Curd is a new substance with a new taste, and milk cannot be got back from it.

o.t: The liquid milk became a semi-solid
o.m: Thought a change in state alone makes a change chemical.

o.t: A new substance with new properties forms and milk cannot be got back
It took a long time to happen
o.m: Thought slow changes are chemical and fast ones are physical.
Thought a change in temperature alone makes a change chemical.

qs.q: Salt is dissolved in water and the water is then evaporated, leaving white salt behind. Dissolving salt in water is a:
qs.why: The salt can be recovered unchanged by evaporation, so no new substance formed. It is a physical change.

o.t: Chemical change, as the salt vanished and was destroyed
o.m: Thought that disappearing in water means the salt was destroyed.

o.t: Chemical change, as evaporation forms a new substance
o.m: Thought evaporation forms a new substance, not just a change of state.

o.t: Physical change, as no new substance forms and salt is recovered
Chemical change, as heat was needed to get the salt back
o.m: Thought any change that needs heat is chemical.

qs.q: The gas produced when vinegar is poured on baking soda is passed through lime water. What is observed?
qs.why: The gas is carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky.

o.m: Expected a colour change as with a litmus test.

o.t: The lime water remains clear because the gas is hydrogen
o.m: Thought the gas is hydrogen and has no effect on lime water.
Thought a chemical change always gives out so much heat.

qs.q: A clean iron nail is kept in blue copper sulphate solution for an hour. What is seen?
qs.why: Iron reacts with copper sulphate: a brown coating of copper forms on the nail and the blue solution turns pale green. New substances form, so it is a chemical change.

o.t: The nail turns blue and the solution becomes a darker blue
o.m: Thought copper sulphate simply sticks to the nail as a physical change.

o.t: A brownish coating on the nail and the blue colour fades to pale green
Nothing happens as iron cannot react with a dissolved substance
o.m: Thought solids cannot react with substances dissolved in water.

o.t: The solution turns red as the nail rusts in it
o.m: Mixed up this reaction with rusting.

qs.q: A fisherman paints the iron body of his boat. How does the paint help?
qs.why: Paint keeps iron away from oxygen and water, which are both needed for rusting.

o.t: It gives the iron extra oxygen to stay strong
o.m: Thought oxygen protects iron when it actually causes rust.

o.t: It changes rust back into iron
o.m: Thought paint can reverse a chemical change.

o.t: It makes the iron hotter so water dries up
o.m: Thought heat from paint dries up the water.

o.t: It stops air and water from touching the iron

qs.q: Which list has only chemical changes?
qs.why: Cooking dal, ripening of mango and rusting form new substances. Each of the other lists contains a physical change.

o.t: Cooking dal, ripening of mango, rusting of a bucket
Boiling water, cooking dal, burning coal
o.m: Thought boiling water to steam forms a new substance.

o.t: Freezing water, ripening of mango, rusting of a bucket
o.m: Thought freezing changes the properties so much that it is chemical.

o.t: Crushing chalk, burning coal, souring of milk
o.m: Thought that crushing chalk forms a new substance.

lesson.title: Speed, time and motion
points: Speed is the distance travelled in one unit of time: speed = distance ÷ time. Its units are metre per second (m/s) or kilometre per hour (km/h).
If an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, its motion is uniform. If not, it is non-uniform.
A pendulum moving to and fro is oscillating. The time for one oscillation is its time period = total time ÷ number of oscillations.
A speedometer in a vehicle shows speed and an odometer shows the distance covered.
lesson.story: Imagine a bus on a highway with kilometre stones. If it crosses 60 stones in 1 hour, it moves at 60 km/h. But in traffic it speeds up and slows down, so its motion is non-uniform.

example.q: A train covers 240 km in 4 hours. Find its speed.
steps: Write the formula: speed = distance ÷ time.
Put the values: speed = 240 km ÷ 4 h.
Speed = 60 km/h.

qs.q: Which of these is a unit of speed?
qs.why: Speed is distance per unit time, so m/s and km/h are its units.

o.m: Gave a unit of distance instead of speed.
Gave a unit of time instead of speed.
Gave a unit of mass instead of speed.

qs.q: The speed of a moving object is found by:
qs.why: Speed is the distance covered in one unit of time, that is distance ÷ time.

o.t: Dividing the time taken by the distance covered
o.m: Turned the formula upside down.

o.t: Dividing the distance covered by the time taken
Multiplying the distance by the time taken
o.m: Multiplied the two quantities instead of dividing.

o.t: Subtracting the time taken from the distance
o.m: Subtracted quantities that have different units.

qs.q: A bus covers 150 km in 3 hours. Its speed is:
qs.why: Speed = 150 km ÷ 3 h = 50 km/h.

o.m: Multiplied distance by time instead of dividing.
Divided time by distance instead of distance by time.
Subtracted time from distance.

qs.q: A pendulum completes 20 oscillations in 40 seconds. Its time period is:
qs.why: Time period = 40 s ÷ 20 = 2 s.

o.m: Multiplied 20 by 40 instead of dividing.
Divided the number of oscillations by the time.
Added the two numbers.

qs.q: A ball rolls 4 m in the 1st second, 4 m in the 2nd second and 4 m in the 3rd second. Its motion is:
qs.why: It covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, so the motion is uniform.

o.t: Non-uniform, because the total distance keeps growing
o.m: Looked at total distance instead of the distance in each second.

o.t: Non-uniform, because it is moving on the ground
o.m: Thought only motion in the air can be uniform.

o.t: Oscillatory, because it repeats the same distance
o.m: Thought repeating equal distances is a to-and-fro motion.

qs.q: Ravi's scooter covers 45 km in 1.5 h and Imran's car covers 80 km in 2 h. Which is faster, and by how much?
qs.why: Scooter: 45 ÷ 1.5 = 30 km/h. Car: 80 ÷ 2 = 40 km/h. The car is faster by 10 km/h.

o.m: Compared only the distances: 80 − 45.

o.t: The scooter, as it took less time
o.m: Compared only the time taken, not the distance.
Divided time by distance and picked the larger value as faster.

qs.q: A cyclist rides at a steady speed of 12 km/h for 30 minutes. The distance covered is:
qs.why: 30 minutes = 0.5 h. Distance = speed × time = 12 × 0.5 = 6 km.

o.m: Multiplied 12 by 30 without changing minutes to hours.
Divided the speed by the time in minutes.
Added speed and time.

qs.q: A car travels 10 km in the first hour, 30 km in the second hour and 20 km in the third hour. Which is correct?
qs.why: Total distance = 60 km in 3 h, so average speed = 20 km/h. Distances in equal hours are different, so it is non-uniform.

o.m: Thought a steady average value means motion is uniform.

o.t: Non-uniform motion; average speed is 30 km/h
o.m: Took the largest distance as the average speed.

o.t: Non-uniform motion; average speed is 20 km/h
Non-uniform motion; average speed is 10 km/h
o.m: Took the first hour's distance as the average speed.

lesson.title: What electric current can do
points: When current flows through a wire, the wire gets hot. This is the heating effect. Electric heaters, irons and toasters use it, and the filament of a bulb glows because it gets very hot.
A fuse is a thin wire that melts if too much current flows, breaking the circuit. This protects the appliances. MCBs now do this job too.
A current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet and deflects a compass needle. This is the magnetic effect, discovered by Oersted.
An electromagnet is an insulated wire coiled around a soft iron piece. It is a magnet only while current flows. Electric bells and cranes use it.
lesson.story: The fuse in a house is like the safety valve of a pressure cooker. When too much current, like too much steam, builds up, the fuse gives way first and protects everything else.

example.q: How can you make an electromagnet?
steps: Take a long insulated copper wire and wind it into a coil around a soft iron nail.
Join the two ends of the wire to a cell through a switch.
When the switch is closed, current flows and the nail behaves like a magnet. When the switch is opened, it loses its magnetism.

qs.q: An electric iron becomes hot when it is switched on. This is due to the:
qs.why: Current flowing through the heating element of the iron makes it hot. This is the heating effect of current.

o.m: Thought a magnet inside the iron makes it hot.

o.t: Friction between the plug pins and the socket
o.m: Thought rubbing of the plug pins makes it hot.

o.t: Light given by the red indicator lamp
o.m: Thought the small indicator lamp heats the iron.

qs.q: Which of these devices works on the magnetic effect of electric current?
qs.why: An electric bell has an electromagnet and so works on the magnetic effect of current.

o.m: Thought every electrical device works by the magnetic effect.
Thought every electrical device works by the magnetic effect.
Mixed up the heating effect with the magnetic effect.

qs.q: Why does the wire in a fuse melt when too much current flows through it?
qs.why: Excess current heats the thin fuse wire, which has a low melting point, so it melts and breaks the circuit.

o.t: Excess current heats the wire so much that it melts and cuts off the supply
Excess current makes the wire a magnet that pulls itself apart

o.t: Too little current cannot keep the wire warm, so it breaks
o.m: Thought the fuse melts when current is low.

o.t: The wire melts as it gets sunlight inside the meter box
o.m: Thought the melting is due to outside heat.

qs.q: Which material is best as the core of an electromagnet?
qs.why: A piece of soft iron is strongly magnetised by the coil and loses it when the current stops.

o.m: Thought a good conductor of electricity makes the best core.
Thought any rod inside the coil works equally well.
Thought an insulator can be magnetised by the coil.

qs.q: A bulb is connected to a cell through a switch which is in the OFF position. The bulb does not glow because:
qs.why: With the switch OFF, the circuit is open (incomplete), so no current flows.

o.t: The cell has stopped working for good
o.m: Thought the cell loses its charge when the switch is OFF.

o.t: The bulb needs more than one cell to glow
o.m: Thought a single cell can never light a bulb.

o.t: Current flows only in the wires, never in the bulb
o.m: Thought the bulb is not part of the path of current.

o.t: The circuit is open, so no current flows

qs.q: Why is an electromagnet, and not a permanent magnet, used in a crane to lift scrap iron?
qs.why: An electromagnet can be switched on to lift the iron and switched off to drop it.

o.t: It can be switched on to lift the iron and off to drop it
A permanent magnet cannot attract iron

o.t: An electromagnet attracts all materials, including wood
o.m: Thought a magnet attracts everything.

o.t: An electromagnet never loses its strength
o.m: Thought an electromagnet keeps its magnetism even when off.

qs.q: In an electric bell, why does the hammer keep striking the gong again and again while the button is pressed?
qs.why: The electromagnet pulls the strip and the hammer hits the gong. This breaks the circuit, the magnet loses its pull and the strip springs back. The circuit is complete again and it repeats.

o.t: The person keeps pressing and releasing the button very fast
o.m: Thought the repeated sound is made by the hand and not by the bell.

o.t: A permanent magnet inside keeps pulling the hammer
o.m: Thought a bell uses a permanent magnet and not an electromagnet.

o.t: Each strike breaks the circuit, the strip springs back and completes it again
The current in the bell keeps changing its direction
o.m: Thought the repeated striking comes from the changing direction of current.

qs.q: A compass needle placed below a wire deflects when the switch is closed and returns to its old position when the switch is opened. This shows:
qs.why: The wire shows magnetic effect only while the current flows.

o.t: The wire became a permanent magnet
o.m: Thought the wire stays magnetised after the current stops.

o.t: The needle was pulled by the cell and not by the wire
o.m: Thought the cell attracts the needle.

o.t: Heat from the wire turned the needle

lesson.title: Reflection and mirrors
points: When light falls on a polished surface it bounces back. This is reflection. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both are measured from the normal.
A plane mirror forms an image that is virtual, upright and of the same size. It is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and left and right are swapped (lateral inversion).

A concave mirror curves inwards and can give an enlarged image. It is used in torches, by dentists and as shaving mirrors. A convex mirror bulges outwards and gives a smaller, upright image with a wide view. It is used as a rear-view mirror.
A virtual image cannot be caught on a screen.
lesson.story: Stand in front of the bathroom mirror and raise your right hand. The image seems to raise its left hand. That is lateral inversion, and it is the reason AMBULANCE is written reversed on vans.

lesson.title: The tiny building blocks of life
points: All living things are made of cells, the basic units of life.
Robert Hooke first saw cells in a slice of cork in 1665. Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus.
Every cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. Plant cells also have a cell wall, plastids (like chloroplasts) and a large vacuole.

lesson.title: Growing up and making new life
points: Reproduction is asexual (one parent, as in budding of Hydra and binary fission of Amoeba) or sexual (male and female gametes fuse).

The zygote becomes an embryo and then a foetus. Animals that lay eggs are oviparous. Those that give birth to young ones are viviparous.
Adolescence (about 11 to 19 years) brings puberty, controlled by hormones. Whether the sperm carries X or Y decides the baby's sex.

lesson.title: Push, pull and press
points: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N). Forces in the same direction add up; forces in opposite directions subtract.

Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact. Rolling friction is less than sliding friction, and lubricants reduce friction.

lesson.title: How things burn
points: Combustion is the burning of a substance in air (oxygen) to give heat and often light. Burning needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat to reach the ignition temperature.
The ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire. Substances with a very low ignition temperature, like petrol and LPG, are highly inflammable.
A candle flame has three zones: the dark inner zone, the middle luminous zone (partial combustion) and the outer non-luminous zone, which is the hottest (complete combustion).
The calorific value of a fuel is the heat in kJ produced by the complete burning of 1 kg of it. Fire is put out by cutting off the air, removing the fuel or cooling below the ignition temperature.
lesson.story: On a chulha, the firewood needs a small flame or a matchstick to start burning, but then it keeps burning on its own. The match heats the wood up to its ignition temperature, and the air supplies oxygen.

example.q: A fuel has a calorific value of 45,000 kJ/kg. How much heat is produced by completely burning 2 kg of it?

So the heat produced is 90,000 kJ.

points: Lavoisier's law of conservation of mass says mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Proust's law of constant proportions says a compound always has its elements in a fixed mass ratio, for example hydrogen to oxygen in water is 1 : 8.

lesson.title: Gravity, work and energy
points: Newton's law of gravitation: every two bodies attract each other with a force F = G m₁m₂ ÷ d². Force grows with the masses and falls with the square of the distance. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg².
Near the Earth all freely falling bodies have the same acceleration g = 9.8 m/s². Mass stays the same everywhere, but weight (mg) on the Moon is about one-sixth of that on Earth.
Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs, in joules. Kinetic energy is ½mv², potential energy is mgh, and energy changes form without being lost.
Power is the rate of doing work, P = W ÷ t, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).
lesson.story: A coconut falling from a tree gains speed as it drops. Its stored energy mgh at the top turns into movement energy ½mv² near the ground.

example.q: A boy lifts a 5 kg bag through 2 m. Find the work done against gravity. (g = 10 m/s²)
steps: The force needed equals the weight: F = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N.
Displacement s = 2 m in the direction of the force.

lesson.title: How sound travels
points: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and travels as a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions. It needs a material medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases, and it moves faster when the temperature rises.
Frequency (Hz) decides the pitch, and amplitude decides the loudness. The wave speed is v = f × λ. Humans hear from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; below this is infrasound and above it is ultrasound.
An echo is the reflection of sound, and the sound must travel to the obstacle and back, so the time is t = 2d ÷ v. SONAR uses ultrasound to measure the depth of the sea.
lesson.story: When you shout towards the walls of an empty hall at your school, your own voice comes back after a short gap. That is an echo, sound bouncing back from the wall.

example.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 200 Hz and a wavelength of 1.7 m. Find its speed.
